startup.name: Robocurve
startup.description:
Robocurve builds open-source tools and independent benchmarks to measure how well robots can do real-world jobs. Instead of relying on unverified demo videos from frontier labs, we score their models on reproducible benchmarks that anyone can trust.

Today there are no well-run, standardized robotics benchmarks. Labs evaluate in-house, and no independent group has stepped in to run continuous benchmarking as a service. The result is that no one actually knows how good anyone else is, or where the real frontier sits.

Good benchmarks require operating and maintaining physical hardware and real-world setups. Simulation only goes so far, since models that look strong in sim can show large performance gaps once deployed in the real world. Building real-world benchmarks means coordinating job-domain experts, evals engineering, and hands-on robotics all at once.

yc_acceptance.basis: Starting rate is about 1 percent with a 0.6 to 2 percent band. The company is already accepted, so this is a note only. Three founders with AI evals and robotics backgrounds, an open source framework already shipped and a pilot done lift the odds, but a thin commercial story holds them back.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC would most plausibly say no because benchmarks are a public good with no clear buyer, and hardware heavy evaluation is slow and expensive. Reviewers would ask who pays, how a three person team keeps physical robots running, and why labs would trust an unproven independent party.

outcomes.why_it_fails: A trusted measure business is likely to stay small or be acquired by a lab, a cloud or a robotics company. A shutdown or stall is the most common result because the buyer set is small and hardware costs are real.

technical_complexity.rationale: Reliable real world evaluation needs maintained robot hardware, scoring that is autonomous and reproducible, and domain tasks. A three person team can run pilots but scaling across robot types and keeping results trusted is hard and capital intensive.

takeover_risk.rationale: Academic groups publish free benchmarks and labs could fund their own, but running continuous independent evaluation as a service requires hardware and ops that few want. Copying is slower than for software.

evidence.claim: Papers argue that standardized low cost real world benchmarks are missing and simulation falls short.
Authors say high scores on traditional benchmarks do not reliably indicate robust embodied intelligence.

brand.name_check: python3 -I scripts/name_features.py --score "Robocurve" --era 2022+ : kind invented_or_proper, 9 chars, 3 syllables
weaknesses: Sounds like a generic robotics name
brand.rationale: A compound that signals robots and measurement is clear but forgettable, much like other descriptive compounds in the YC data. Credibility as a neutral referee will rest on results, not the name.

narrative.headline: A well timed independent robotics evals company with a plausible seed but a hard path to paying customers and later rounds.
narrative.general_summary: Robocurve builds open source tools and independent benchmarks for robots. The need is real because academic papers confirm that real world evaluation is scarce. But buyers are few, hardware is costly, and benchmarks tend to be free. A seed above the YC deal is more likely than not given the robotics and eval interest, but later steps are hard and the anecdotal robotics cohort has no Series A yet.

assumptions: Blind test: only the batch input file was used for the company.
A seed here means a round above the YC deal of about 500K within about 12 months of the batch start.
Robotics and Industrials cohorts have under 30 companies, so rates are anecdotes.
